name: Umāsvāti
summary: Author of the Tattvārthasūtra, the first Sanskrit summa of Jain doctrine, accepted by both sects. The Śvetāmbaras know him as Umāsvāti, son of Svāti and Umā, of the Uccairnāgara branch, who also wrote the bhāṣya and the Praśamarati; the Digambaras as Umāsvāmin (also called Gṛdhrapiccha), in Kundakunda's line.
notes: His Praśamarati (Śvetāmbara) is not given a separate entry here (gap).

name: Pūjyapāda Devanandin
summary: Digambara ācārya, grammarian and philosopher: author of the Sarvārthasiddhi (which fixed the Digambara Tattvārthasūtra), the Samādhitantra and Iṣṭopadeśa on the self, and the Jainendra grammar.

name: Akalaṅka

realization_account.text: Victory in debate over the Buddhists at Kāñcī, where Tārā spoke from behind a curtain until he exposed her (legend).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Digambara logician who gave Jain epistemology its classical form (the conventionally direct and truly direct perception; memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture as indirect knowledge) and wrote the Tattvārtharājavārttika. The tradition tells that he studied in a Buddhist monastery in disguise with his brother Niṣkalaṅka, who was killed, and later defeated the Buddhists in debate at the court of Himaśītala at Kāñcī, where the goddess Tārā spoke behind a curtain.

name: Vidyānanda
summary: Digambara logician, author of the Tattvārthaślokavārttika, the Aṣṭasahasrī on the Āptamīmāṃsā and the Āptaparīkṣā, defending the omniscient teacher and refuting the creator God.

name: Siddhasenagaṇi
summary: Śvetāmbara commentator on the Tattvārthasūtra and its bhāṣya.

name: Samantabhadra

tradition.text: often placed in the 2nd c. CE

realization_account.text: The image of Candraprabha emerged from the liṅga at Vārāṇasī as he sang the hymn to the eighth Tīrthaṅkara.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Digambara poet-philosopher who first set out many-sidedness and the sevenfold predication systematically in the Āptamīmāṃsā, and wrote the Svayambhūstotra, Yuktyanuśāsana and (by tradition) the Ratnakaraṇḍaśrāvakācāra. The tradition tells that he was afflicted by an insatiable hunger (bhasmaka), took leave of monkhood to cure it, and at Vārāṇasī caused the image of Candraprabha to appear from a Śiva-liṅga while reciting his hymn.

name: Siddhasena Divākara

realization_account.text: Pārśvanātha's image emerged from the liṅga at the Mahākāla temple when he recited his hymn (legend).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Logician-poet revered by both sects: author of the Prakrit Sanmatitarka on the standpoints and of hymns (dvātriṃśikās); the Nyāyāvatāra and Kalyāṇamandira are ascribed to him (disputed). He held that in the omniscient knowledge and perception are one. The tradition tells that he proposed rendering the Prakrit scriptures into Sanskrit, was sent into twelve years' exile for it, and during it made Pārśva's image appear at the Mahākāla temple of Ujjain, converting king Vikramāditya.

name: Mallavādin
summary: Śvetāmbara dialectician, author of the Dvādaśāranayacakra; the tradition says he defeated the Buddhists in debate at Valabhī.

name: Siṃhasūri Gaṇi (Vādikṣamāśramaṇa)
summary: Śvetāmbara commentator on Mallavādin's Nayacakra.

name: Jinabhadra Gaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa
summary: Śvetāmbara scholastic, author of the Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya (with the Gaṇadharavāda) and, by tradition, the Dhyānaśataka; defender of the view that the omniscient's knowledge and perception occur in sequence.

name: Māṇikyanandi
summary: Digambara logician, author of the Parīkṣāmukha.

name: Prabhācandra
summary: Digambara logician of Dhārā, author of the Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa and Nyāyakumudacandra, which argue against the Śvetāmbara-Yāpanīya positions that the kevalin eats and that women can be liberated.

name: Vādidevasūri
summary: Śvetāmbara logician of Gujarat, author of the Pramāṇanayatattvāloka and Syādvādaratnākara; the tradition tells of his debate victory over the Digambara Kumudacandra at Siddharāja's court (1125).

name: Haribhadra Sūri
summary: Śvetāmbara ācārya and the great systematizer of Jain yoga (Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, Yogabindu, Yogaśataka, Yogaviṃśikā), doxographer of all the darśanas (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, Śāstravārtāsamuccaya) and polemicist. The tradition tells that he was a learned brahmin of Citrakūṭa who vowed to become the pupil of anyone whose words he could not understand; hearing the nun Yākinī recite a verse he could not explain, he took initiation and called himself 'Yākinī's spiritual son'. After his pupils Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa were killed by Buddhists, his anger was calmed by his teacher; he is credited with 1,444 works, many signed with the word 'viraha' (separation).
notes: Several different authors named Haribhadra existed; the ascription of some of the 1,444 works is doubtful.

name: Yākinī Mahattarā
summary: Śvetāmbara nun (mahattarā, senior nun) whose recitation of a verse Haribhadra could not understand led to his conversion; he honoured her as his spiritual mother.

name: Hemacandra

realization_account.text: He says the twelfth chapter of the Yogaśāstra sets out what is 'established by experience' (anubhavasiddha), beyond what he learned from scripture and the teacher.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Śvetāmbara polymath of Gujarat ('Kalikālasarvajña', the omniscient of the Kali age), teacher of king Kumārapāla, for whom he wrote the Yogaśāstra; also author of the Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, the Vītarāgastotra, the two Vyavacchedikā hymns, the Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacarita, and works on grammar and poetics. He declares that the last chapter of the Yogaśāstra rests on his own experience.

name: Devacandra Sūri (teacher of Hemacandra)
summary: Śvetāmbara monk who initiated the boy Cāṅgadeva as Somacandra (later Hemacandra).
notes: Distinct from the 18th-c. Kharatara author Devacandra (tch:devacandra-kharatara).

name: Malliṣeṇa (author of the Syādvādamañjarī)
summary: Śvetāmbara monk of the Nāgendra-gaccha, author of the Syādvādamañjarī (1292).
notes: Distinct from the Digambara Malliṣeṇa of the Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa.

name: Śubhacandra (author of the Jñānārṇava)

tradition.text: time of king Muñja/Bhoja of Dhārā

summary: Digambara ācārya, author of the Jñānārṇava on meditation. The tradition tells that he and his brother Bhartṛhari were princes who renounced; Bhartṛhari became a yogin who gained an alchemical elixir, and Śubhacandra showed him that self-knowledge, not the elixir, is the true attainment — the Jñānārṇava being written for his instruction.

name: Yaśovijaya
summary: Śvetāmbara (Tapā Gaccha) monk-scholar ('Nyāyaviśārada', 'Upādhyāya') who studied Navya-Nyāya at Vārāṇasī and wrote over a hundred works in Sanskrit, Prakrit and Gujarati: on logic and standpoints (Jaina Tarkabhāṣā, Nayopadeśa, Jñānabindu), on adhyātma and yoga (Adhyātmasāra, Adhyātmopaniṣad, Jñānasāra, a commentary on the Yoga Sūtra, dvātriṃśikās), and a critique of Banārsīdās's Adhyātma circle. The tradition tells that he met Ānandaghana and praised him in eight verses.

name: Vinayavijaya
summary: Śvetāmbara monk, fellow-student of Yaśovijaya, author of the Lokaprakāśa and of the Śrīpāla-rāsa completed by Yaśovijaya.

name: Devendrasūri
summary: Tapā Gaccha ācārya, author of the new Karmagranthas.

name: Ratnaśekhara Sūri
summary: Śvetāmbara author to whom the Guṇasthānakramāroha is ascribed.
notes: Identity with other Ratnaśekharas (e.g. the author of the Sirisirivālakahā) not established.

name: Yogīndu

scholarly.text: c. 6th c. CE (some: up to the 10th c.)

summary: Digambara mystic poet in Apabhraṃśa, author of the Paramātmaprakāśa and the Yogasāra, teaching that the soul in its essence is the supreme self.

name: Rāmasiṃha Muni
summary: Digambara author of the Apabhraṃśa Pāhuḍa Dohā, critic of outer ritual.

name: Amitagati (II)
summary: Digambara author of the Yogasāraprābhṛta, the Subhāṣitaratnasaṃdoha and (by tradition) the Sāmāyikapāṭha.

name: Svāmi Kārttikeya
summary: Author of the Prakrit Kārttikeyānuprekṣā on the twelve reflections.

name: Nemicandra Siddhāntacakravartin
summary: Digambara ācārya of Karnataka, author of the Gommaṭasāra (for the general Cāmuṇḍarāya, who erected the Bāhubali colossus at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa), the Labdhisāra, the Trilokasāra and (by tradition) the Dravyasaṃgraha.
notes: Some scholars assign the Dravyasaṃgraha to a different Nemicandra (Siddhāntideva).

name: Yativṛṣabha
summary: Digambara author of the Tiloyapaṇṇatti and of cūrṇi-sūtras on the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

name: Vaṭṭakera
summary: Name under which the Mūlācāra is transmitted.

name: Śivārya
summary: Author of the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā on the four propitiations and the good death.

name: Somadeva Sūri
summary: Digambara author of the Yaśastilaka (959) including its Upāsakādhyayana, and of the Nītivākyāmṛta.

name: Amṛtacandra Sūri
summary: Digambara commentator whose Ātmakhyāti (with its kalaśa verses) made Kundakunda's Samayasāra the charter of the niścaya-centred path; also author of the Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya and commentaries on the Pravacanasāra and Pañcāstikāya.

name: Jayasena (commentator)
summary: Digambara commentator on Kundakunda's works (Tātparyavṛtti).

name: Guṇabhadra
summary: Digambara ācārya, pupil of Jinasena; author of the Ātmānuśāsana and the Uttarapurāṇa.

name: Jinasena
summary: Digambara ācārya, author of the Ādipurāṇa (U35 cites its argument against a creator).

name: Padmanandi (author of the Pañcaviṃśatikā)
summary: Digambara author of the Padmanandi-pañcaviṃśatikā.

name: Devasena
summary: Digambara author of the Darśanasāra (933), Ārādhanāsāra, Tattvasāra and Ālāpapaddhati.

name: Paṇḍita Āśādhara
summary: Digambara lay scholar of Malwa, author of the Sāgāra- and Anagāra-dharmāmṛta.

name: Śrutasāgara Sūri
summary: Digambara commentator of the 16th c. (Tattvārthavṛtti, commentary on the Aṣṭapāhuḍa).

name: Vasunandi
summary: Digambara author of a śrāvakācāra and of commentaries (on the Āptamīmāṃsā and Mūlācāra).

name: Rāmasena (or Nāgasena)
summary: Name under which the Tattvānuśāsana is transmitted (ascription disputed).

name: Bhaṭṭāraka Jñānabhūṣaṇa
summary: Digambara bhaṭṭāraka, author of the Tattvajñānataraṅgiṇī.

name: Malliṣeṇa (author of the Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa)
summary: Digambara ācārya of Karnataka ('poet-emperor of two languages'), author of the Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa and other mantra works.

name: Indranandi
summary: Digambara author of the Jvālāmālinī-kalpa (939); a (possibly different) Indranandi wrote the Śrutāvatāra.

name: Mānatuṅga

realization_account.text: The chains fell away one by one as he sang the Bhaktāmara.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Author of the Bhaktāmara-stotra; the tradition says that when a king (Bhoja or Harṣa in different versions) had him bound in forty-four (or forty-eight) chains, each verse of the hymn broke one.

name: Siṃhatilaka Sūri
summary: Śvetāmbara author of works on the Sūrimantra and the Vardhamāna-vidyā.

name: Jinaprabha Sūri
summary: Kharatara Gaccha ācārya, author of the Vividhatīrthakalpa and of works on the Sūrimantra; the tradition tells of his wonders at the court of Muhammad bin Tughluq.

name: Ānandaghana
summary: Śvetāmbara (Tapā Gaccha) monk who became a wandering mystic poet; author of the Covīsī hymns to the Tīrthaṅkaras and of the Bahottarī padas. He sings the soul's love for the Jina, dismisses sectarian dispute and treats the six darśanas as limbs of the Jina. The tradition identifies him with the monk Lābhānanda, says he lived and died at Meṛtā, and that Yaśovijaya sought him out and praised him.

name: Devacandra (Kharatara Gaccha)
summary: Śvetāmbara monk-poet of the Kharatara Gaccha, author of philosophical Gujarati hymns (Covīsī), the Adhyātmagītā and the Nayacakrasāra.

name: Meghavijaya
summary: Tapā Gaccha monk-scholar who wrote the Yuktiprabodha against the Adhyātma ('Vāṇārasīya') view.

name: Cidānanda (Kapūrcand)
summary: Śvetāmbara mystic poet of the 19th c., author of the Cidānanda Bahottarī and (by tradition) a Svarodaya.

name: Pāṇḍe Rājamalla
summary: Digambara lay scholar whose Hindi (Ḍhūṇḍhārī) commentary on Amṛtacandra's Samayasāra-kalaśas was the text through which Banārsīdās came to the Samayasāra; author (by tradition) of the Pañcādhyāyī and of the Lāṭīsaṃhitā and Adhyātmakamalamārtaṇḍa.

name: Banārsīdās

realization_account.text: After studying the guṇasthānas with Rūpcand he says his understanding became balanced and he held niścaya and vyavahāra together (Ardhakathānaka).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Śrīmāl merchant-poet of Jaunpur and Agra (1587–c. 1643), founder figure of the Adhyātma movement; author of the Samayasāra Nāṭaka and of the Ardhakathānaka, the first autobiography in Hindi. Born into a Śvetāmbara (Kharatara) family, he turned to the Digambara Samayasāra; by his own account he first fell into disregard of conduct and was restored to balance by Rūpcand Pāṇḍe's teaching of the guṇasthānas.

name: Rūpcand Pāṇḍe
summary: Digambara scholar at Agra who taught Banārsīdās and his friends the Gommaṭasāra and the guṇasthānas (1635).

name: Hemrāj Pāṇḍe
summary: Hindi prose commentator (bālāvabodha) on the Pravacanasāra and other Digambara works, in Banārsīdās's circle.

name: Dyānatrāy
summary: Hindi Digambara poet of Agra and Delhi (c. 1676–1726), author of pūjās and adhyātma padas.

name: Bhūdhardās
summary: Hindi Digambara poet of Agra (Jain Śatak, Pārśvapurāṇa).

name: Ṭoḍarmal
summary: Digambara lay scholar of Jaipur (c. 1719–1767), leading figure of the Digambara Terāpantha, author of the Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka and of the Hindi commentary Samyagjñānacandrikā on the Gommaṭasāra; the tradition says he was executed at Jaipur as a result of sectarian hostility.

name: Daulatrām (author of the Chahḍhālā)
summary: Hindi Digambara poet (1798–1866), author of the Chahḍhālā (1834).

name: Śrīmad Rājacandra

realization_account.text: Memory of former lives (jātismaraṇa) at seven; later accounts in his letters of self-realization (samyagdarśana).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Gujarati jeweller, poet and lay teacher (1867–1901), author of the Ātmasiddhi, the Apūrva Avasara and the Mokṣamāḷā; he taught a non-sectarian path of self-realization under a true teacher and was a guide of M. K. Gandhi. The tradition says he recalled past lives from the age of seven, was a prodigy of memory (śatāvadhāna), and attained self-realization; his followers later formed several ashrams (e.g. Agas, Dharampur).
notes: Affinity with the Adhyātma current (he taught from the Samayasāra and Banārsīdās's Nāṭaka) rather than formal membership.

name: Lallujī Muni (Laghurāj Svāmī)
summary: Sthānakavāsī monk (1856–1936) who became Śrīmad Rājacandra's disciple and founded the Agas ashram.

name: Saubhāgbhāī (Sobhāgbhāī) of Sāyalā
summary: Close disciple of Śrīmad Rājacandra, for whom (with others) the Ātmasiddhi was written.

name: Bhadrabāhu
summary: U35 contribution: the Śvetāmbara tradition ascribes the protective hymn Uvasaggaharaṃ to Bhadrabāhu (in the later legend, a brother of the astrologer Varāhamihira).

name: Indrabhūti Gautama
summary: U35 contribution: chief disciple (gaṇadhara) of Mahāvīra, to whom the Ṛṣimaṇḍala-stotra is traditionally ascribed; in the Gaṇadharavāda his doubt about the existence of the soul is resolved by Mahāvīra.
